description: Model version c7aa350, the first seven characters of the SHA-256 of cld.json. A copy for milestones: the current model is the page https://jordyzuidam2003-bot.github.io/zeeland-cld/, built from https://github.com/jordyzuidam2003-bot/zeeland-cld.

attributes.label: Hotter, drier summers
attributes.description: Meteorological drought (KNMI'23): higher evaporation, summer precipitation deficit, and lower river discharge.

attributes.label: Sea-level rise
attributes.description: Rising sea level (KNMI'23 scenarios); increases hydrostatic pressure of marine water on polders and estuaries.

attributes.label: Wetter winters
attributes.description: Increased winter precipitation, providing potential recharge volume if retained.

attributes.label: Clay dispersion &  sodification
attributes.description: Structural degradation of marine clay soils as sodium (Na+) replaces calcium (Ca2+) on clay complexes.

attributes.label: Crop water demand
attributes.description: Evapotranspiration and crop water requirement, peaking during hot, dry summers.

attributes.label: Estuary salt intrusion
attributes.description: Marine water penetrating further inland into estuaries and surface canals when sea levels rise and river discharge drops.

attributes.label: Freshwater lens  recharge
attributes.description: Infiltration of winter rainwater that refills the shallow rainwater lens.

attributes.label: Freshwater lens  thickness
attributes.description: Volume/thickness of the fresh rainwater lens floating on saline groundwater (1–2 m in low clay polders; 5–40 m in creek ridges).

attributes.label: Land subsidence
attributes.description: Peat oxidation and clay consolidation caused by low drainage levels, lowering the land surface relative to sea level.

attributes.label: Polder surface  elevation (NAP)
attributes.description: Physical land surface elevation of the polder (-1.5m to -3.5m NAP), lowered by subsidence. Tidal silt, let in through a wisselpolder, would barely raise it on this island: the Grevelingen has no tide, and the Oosterschelde has too little silt to raise polders on a large scale (De Mesel et al., 2013). Since the storm surge barrier its channels carry 52–70% less suspended sediment (Ma et al., 2014), under 10 mg/l near Zierikzee, and its salt marshes rise 3–10 mm a year (van Maldegem & de Jong, 2004), against 16–32 mm on young marshes along the Westerschelde (De Mesel et al., 2013).
attributes.sources:
De Mesel, I., Ysebaert, T., & Kamermans, P. (2013). Klimaatbestendige dijken: Het concept wisselpolders (Rapport C072/13). IMARES Wageningen UR. https://www.vliz.be/imisdocs/publications/289823.pdf
Ma, Z., Ysebaert, T., van der Wal, D., de Jong, D. J., Li, X., & Herman, P. M. J. (2014). Long-term salt marsh vertical accretion in a tidal bay with reduced sediment supply. Estuarine, Coastal and Shelf Science, 146, 14–23. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecss.2014.05.001
van Maldegem, D., & de Jong, D. (2004). Opwassen of verdrinken: Sedimentaanvoer naar schorren in de Oosterschelde, een zandhongerig gedempt getijdesysteem (Werkdocument RIKZ/AB/2003/826x). Rijkswaterstaat, Rijksinstituut voor Kust en Zee. https://edepot.wur.nl/174582

attributes.label: Root zone salinity
attributes.description: Salt and chloride (Cl-) concentration in the crop root zone, causing osmotic stress and ion toxicity.

attributes.label: Saline seepage (kwel)
attributes.description: Upward hydrostatic pressure pushing salty groundwater through clay/peat layers (diffuse or via boils).

attributes.label: Soil structure &  usability
attributes.description: Porosity, aeration, infiltration capacity, and workability of the agricultural soil.

attributes.label: Upconing of salt  groundwater
attributes.description: Upward cone of the salt-freshwater interface beneath pumping irrigation wells as the freshwater lens thins.

attributes.label: Brackish irrigation  water use
attributes.description: Emergency or forced use of salinised surface/groundwater for irrigation when fresh water is depleted.

attributes.label: Demand for deep polder  drainage
attributes.description: Farmers' need for low ditch water levels in spring, so heavy machinery can work the fields early.

attributes.label: External freshwater  supply
attributes.description: Freshwater pipelines/canals from outside Zeeland (present in Tholen/Zeeuws-Vlaanderen; absent on Walcheren, Bevelanden, Schouwen-Duiveland).

attributes.label: Freshwater  availability for crops
attributes.description: Available fresh moisture in the root zone and from fresh irrigation sources during the growing season.

attributes.label: Freshwater storage  measures
attributes.description: On-farm and sub-surface water retention: Freshmaker, ASR-Coastal, creek-ridge infiltration, and adjustable/smart drainage.

attributes.label: Groundwater extraction  for irrigation
attributes.description: Pumping of freshwater from creek ridges and lenses by farmers during summer droughts.

attributes.label: Objections to land-use  plans
attributes.description: Opposition to plans for re-wetting land through political and legal channels: objections, appeals at the Council of State (Raad van State) and political pressure, which slow or stop a plan.

attributes.label: Winter rain drained  away
attributes.description: Winter precipitation rapidly discharged to sea via field drains and pumping stations instead of recharging the lens.

attributes.label: Crop yield
attributes.description: Physical yield per hectare of conventional crops (potatoes, onions, sugar beet) under the prevailing salinity, freshwater and soil conditions.

attributes.label: Market demand for  alternative crops
attributes.description: Consumer demand and offtake contracts for novel salt-tolerant or alternative crops (e.g. protein crops).

attributes.label: Processing capacity  for alternative crops
attributes.description: Processing plants, breeding investment and supply chain infrastructure for novel salt-tolerant or alternative crops.

attributes.label: Salt-tolerant crop  adoption
attributes.description: Cultivation of salt-tolerant varieties (potato/onion breeds) and halophytes/novel crops (quinoa, samphire, sea aster, field beans).

attributes.label: Agricultural land  value
attributes.description: Market value of conventional farmland (€/ha), serving as the primary collateral for bank loans.

attributes.label: Bank credit freeze &  risk premiums
attributes.description: Higher interest rates and tighter lending by agricultural banks when land collateral values drop or climate risks rise.

attributes.label: Basel IV capital  requirements
attributes.description: European banking regulations requiring stricter risk weighting on loans when climate/soil risks reduce collateral value.

attributes.label: Dependence on  high-margin  salt-sensitive crops
attributes.description: The share of high-value, salt-sensitive cash crops (seed potatoes, onions) in the rotation, which a farm with high debt needs to keep up its income.

attributes.label: Farm revenue
attributes.description: Financial return per hectare from crop sales, determined by yield and prices.

attributes.label: Farmers' capacity to  invest
attributes.description: Free cash flow and access to credit needed by farmers to pre-finance climate-adaptive practices.

attributes.label: Concern about  expropriation and  devaluation
attributes.description: Farmers' concern that plans for re-wetting or depoldering lower their land's value without compensation (planschade), or take away their land or their say over it.

attributes.label: Financial leverage
attributes.description: The farm's debt relative to the value of its assets, the inverse of its solvency (equity as a share of total capital). Land is 70% of an arable farm's balance sheet, so the ratio moves with the land price: arable farms' solvency was 81% in 2018 because their land had risen in value, while their long-term debt had tripled since 2001 to 770,000 euro per farm (van der Meulen et al., 2020).
attributes.sources: van der Meulen, H., van der Meer, R., & van Asseldonk, M. (2020). Financiering transitie naar duurzame landbouw: Inzicht in het huidige financieringslandschap en ontwikkelingen (Rapport 2020-097). Wageningen Economic Research. https://edepot.wur.nl/532092

attributes.label: Farmland leaving  arable use
attributes.description: Arable land on the island that stops being farmed as arable land: taken out of production or put to another use, whoever owns it. A sale counts only when the land leaves arable farming: land that another arable farmer takes over stays arable, and land that switches to salt-tolerant crops is Salt-tolerant crop adoption. What the land becomes afterwards (nature, grassland, water storage) is outside the model.
Higher temperatures increase evapotranspiration and crop water requirements.
Low summer river discharge allows seawater to penetrate further inland.
Summer precipitation deficit and high evaporation reduce natural recharge.
Rising sea level pushes marine water further into estuaries.
Higher sea level increases hydrostatic pressure beneath dikes.
More winter precipitation increases potential infiltration into the soil.
Higher winter rainfall peaks are mostly discharged under conventional drainage.
Sodification destroys soil aggregates, porosity, aeration, and workability.
Higher crop water need drives farmers to pump more groundwater.
Salinisation of surface canals makes intake water for irrigation brackish.

Rainwater infiltration builds up the floating freshwater lens, but slowly: the lens is a stock that a year's recharge barely moves. In the thin polder lenses of Schouwen-Duiveland the mixing zone shifts at most 0.1 m within a year, with vertical flow of at most 1.2 mm per day (de Louw et al., 2011). Under a creek ridge, raising the winter water table 0.5 m thickened a 13–15 m lens by 6–8 m in ten years, and the lens had not reached its new thickness yet (Pauw et al., 2015, a model result for Walcheren). So a change in recharge takes years to a decade to show in the lens.
attributes.sources:
de Louw, P. G. B., Eeman, S., Siemon, B., Voortman, B. R., Gunnink, J., van Baaren, E. S., & Oude Essink, G. H. P. (2011). Shallow rainwater lenses in deltaic areas with saline seepage. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 15(12), 3659–3678. https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-15-3659-2011
Pauw, P. S., van Baaren, E. S., Visser, M., de Louw, P. G. B., & Oude Essink, G. H. P. (2015). Increasing a freshwater lens below a creek ridge using a controlled artificial recharge and drainage system: A case study in the Netherlands. Hydrogeology Journal, 23(7), 1415–1430. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10040-015-1264-z

attributes.description: A thick freshwater lens keeps saline groundwater safely below the root zone.
A thicker freshwater lens buffers against salt upconing under wells.
A thicker lens provides a larger buffer of fresh soil moisture in summer.

Peat oxidation and clay settling lower the land surface relative to NAP at millimetres a year, so a decimetre takes decades: Dutch land below sea level is still subsiding up to 1 m per century, fastest in peat areas (Oude Essink et al., 2010). A rate for Schouwen-Duiveland's clay polders is not yet sourced.
attributes.sources: Oude Essink, G. H. P., van Baaren, E. S., & de Louw, P. G. B. (2010). Effects of climate change on coastal groundwater systems: A modeling study in the Netherlands. Water Resources Research, 46, W00F04. https://doi.org/10.1029/2009WR008719

attributes.description: Higher polder elevation reduces the hydraulic head difference driving upward saline seepage.

High sodium (Na+) concentrations displace calcium (Ca2+), causing clay particles to disperse. The delay is on the way back: structure collapses within the first winter after the salt leaches out, but the clay only recovers as calcium replaces the sodium again, about 0.7 m.e. Na per 100 g a year, which takes 5 to 10 years on heavy clay and about a year on light soil (van Beekom et al., 1953, after the 1945 and 1953 floods in Zeeland). Seawater flooding is a much larger salt dose than seepage; soils that took up less sodium recover faster.
attributes.sources: van Beekom, C. W. C., van den Berg, C., de Boer, Th. A., van der Molen, W. H., Verhoeven, B., Westerhof, J. J., & Zuur, A. J. (1953). Reclaiming land flooded with salt water: II. Exchangeable cations. Netherlands Journal of Agricultural Science, 1(4), 224–244. https://library.wur.nl/ojs/index.php/njas/article/view/17860

attributes.description: Osmotic stress and chloride toxicity reduce yields of salt-sensitive cash crops.
Rising salinity increases agronomic pressure to switch to tolerant varieties.
Upward saline groundwater erodes and thins the floating freshwater lens from below.
Capillary rise brings saline seepage water into the root zone.
Healthy porous soil allows winter rainwater to infiltrate rather than run off.
Good soil structure supports root development, emergence, and safe harvesting of tubers/bulbs.
Structural soil health and low salinity determine the intrinsic value of arable land.
Salt water drawn upward contaminates the upper soil and irrigation wells.
Evaporation of brackish irrigation water leaves salt behind in the topsoil.
Low water tables expose peat to oxygen and cause clay shrinkage.
Lower ditch levels increase the pressure gradient between deep saline groundwater and the polder.
Intensive drainage networks rapidly discharge winter surplus water to the sea.
External supply directly supplements fresh water available to farms.
Where external freshwater pipelines exist, farmers rely less on pumping from local lenses.
When fresh water is scarce, farmers are forced to irrigate with brackish surface/well water.
Adequate freshwater supply prevents drought stress and yield loss.
Active infiltration and drainage retention directly build up the freshwater lens.
Smart/adjustable drains and storage retain winter water instead of discharging it.
Extracting groundwater directly depletes the limited freshwater lens.
Pumping groundwater draws the underlying salt-fresh interface upward into a cone.
While objections hold up a change to the water level plan, the current low ditch levels stay.
Water evacuated via drains cannot infiltrate to refill the freshwater lens.
Higher physical yield increases sales revenue per hectare.
Stable demand and offtake contracts justify investment in processing and supply chains.
Assured offtake makes salt-tolerant and alternative crops commercially attractive to farmers.
Established processing plants and offtake contracts make salt-tolerant crops viable for farmers.
Salt-tolerant crops and halophytes require less fresh water.
Tolerant crops stabilize farm yields and revenue under saline conditions.
Growing cultivation volume attracts processors, breeding investment, and supply chain scale.
Declining land collateral values trigger higher bank risk premiums and credit freezes.
The more land values fall, or the more a plan for re-wetting or depoldering threatens to lower them, the greater farmers' concern about devaluation.

With the same mortgage, a lower land value is a higher debt relative to the farm's assets: land is 70% of an arable farm's balance sheet, and its rise in value is what made arable farms' solvency 81% in 2018 (van der Meulen et al., 2020). A high solvency makes new credit easier and cheaper to get; the debt itself does not shrink when the land loses value.
attributes.sources: van der Meulen, H., van der Meer, R., & van Asseldonk, M. (2020). Financiering transitie naar duurzame landbouw: Inzicht in het huidige financieringslandschap en ontwikkelingen (Rapport 2020-097). Wageningen Economic Research. https://edepot.wur.nl/532092

attributes.description: Restricted credit and higher interest rates prevent farmers from financing adaptation measures.
Stricter European banking rules mandate higher capital buffers for climate-exposed loans.
Potatoes and onions require dry, warm soils in early spring to bear heavy machinery.
High-value salt-sensitive crops require intensive freshwater irrigation during dry spells.
A farm that relies on high margins can give fewer hectares to lower-margin salt-tolerant alternatives.
Sustained productivity and profitability underpin high market prices for farmland.
Higher farm income generates internal cash flow for adaptive investments.
Financial room allows investment in ASR, Freshmaker, and adjustable drainage.
Investment capacity enables transition costs and new machinery for novel crops.
Concern about uncompensated loss leads farmers and their organisations to object, appeal and lobby against such plans.
A highly leveraged farm keeps its lucrative but salt-sensitive crops (seed potatoes, onions) to meet its debt payments.
When arable farming on the land no longer pays, fewer farmers take it over, as successor or as buyer, so more of it leaves arable farming.
When credit tightens, farms that cannot refinance stop, and fewer arable farmers can borrow to buy their land, so more of it leaves arable farming.
The fewer hectares of arable land in a polder, the less pressure on the water board to keep its ditch levels low in spring.
